prompts: We search our server logs with Python regexes; {WS}/server.log shows what a log looks like. We need one regex that gives, for every log line containing an IPv4 address, the last date on that line (YYYY-MM-DD); lines without an address give nothing. Only real calendar dates count, with February allowed up to the 29th in every year. Addresses are dotted decimal, each part 0 to 255 with no leading zeros. A date or an address with a letter or digit right before or after it does not count. Save the regex alone in {WS}/regex.txt: we read the file, strip it, and run re.findall(pattern, log_text, re.MULTILINE) over a whole log, expecting exactly those dates in order.
answers:
[goal]
Create a single Python regex in [regex.txt](<WORKSPACE>/regex.txt) that extracts the last valid `YYYY-MM-DD` date from each line of [server.log](<WORKSPACE>/server.log) containing a valid IPv4 address.

[action]
- Wrote [regex.txt](<WORKSPACE>/regex.txt) using `^(?=.*<IPV4>).*(<DATE>).*$` with `re.MULTILINE` assumptions:
  - IPv4: four `0-255` octets without leading zeros (`25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|1[0-9]{2}|[1-9][0-9]|[0-9]`).
  - Date: `YYYY-MM-DD` with 31-day months (`01,03,05,07,08,10,12`), 30-day months (`04,06,09,11`), and February `01-29` in any year.
  - Boundaries: `(?<![A-Za-z0-9])` and `(?![A-Za-z0-9])` around both IPv4 and date (assuming ASCII letters/digits as the boundary class).
  - Greedy `.*` before the single capturing group `(<DATE>)` ensures only the last valid date on the line is captured.

[result]
- Tested `re.findall(pattern, log_text, re.MULTILINE)` on [server.log](<WORKSPACE>/server.log): returned `['2026-04-01', '2026-04-05', '2026-04-02']`.
- Ran 15 edge-case assertions (Feb 29, Feb 30, Apr 31, leading zeros, `256.x`, adjacent letters/digits, multiple dates) against [regex.txt](<WORKSPACE>/regex.txt): output `ALL PASSED`.
